decision.quote: This study confirms several patterns that have emerged in previous work ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ; Parise & Csibra, 2012 ; Tincoff & Jusczyk, 1999 , 2012 ). Namely, we find further evidence, with a new sample of infants and a new set of item pairs, that 6-9 month olds understand words. Not unexpectedly, this ability increases with age, but perhaps less expectedly the rate with which it increases is non-linear. This is the third study that finds evidence of a boost in performance around 13-14 months, independent of word type ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ). We find three possible explanations for this boost viable. First, this is around the time that infants begin talking ( Dale & Fenson, 1996 ), which may increase their metalinguistic awareness, or understanding of words as community-wide symbols in a way that boosts comprehension . Second, this is just before the time that infants begin to show basic syntactic knowledge, and this in turn may help them use the distribution of arguments in the sentence to listen more predictively ( Jin & Fisher, 2014 ). decision.reason: The complete Parise/Csibra original was independently recovered and inspected. Its specific empirical diagnostic is a word-object congruency N400 response, interpreted as referential semantic understanding rather than mere audiovisual association, present for live maternal but not yoked unfamiliar speech. The current report positively acknowledges this evidence and jointly confirms the broader early-word-comprehension pattern. Its own paired-video looking test, including live parental naming, however does not test the congruent/incongruent semantic-violation response, referential-versus-associative distinction or maternal-versus-unfamiliar speaker claim. It explicitly defines its empirical retest as common-noun comprehension across a wider set of paired moving referents, already represented by Bergelson/Swingley2012 and the directly extended Tincoff/Jusczyk2012 common-noun comparison. No later report is declared an intervening replication of Parise merely from timing or citation. This exclusion rests on the actual original-specific semantic-violation finding and current selected behavioral claim, not on EEG versus gaze measurement alone or omission of one experimental arm. The affirmative collective Discussion wording and current live-parent protocol are preserved as contrary context; no N400 result or semantic-mechanism finding is inferred from ordinary looking preference.
